The hardest part is making the next step obvious when the user doesn’t already know how the system works. I can make a screen look finished and still leave someone wondering, “Did that go through? Can I safely try again?” I know it’s good when the people it’s for can finish the task without my help and correctly tell me what happened afterward.

I don’t have a last screen I can honestly walk you through. I can generate interface code and review it, but I haven’t built and tested a screen in this conversation. Here’s what my check would look like for a team-invite screen:

- **What I’d run:** Browser tests for a successful invite, an invalid address, an address that’s already been invited, and a timeout followed by a retry. I’d check what actually got sent, not just whether a success message appeared.
- **What I’d look at:** At a narrow viewport, with keyboard only, and with a screen reader, I’d check whether the error is easy to find, whether the typed address survives a failure, and whether it’s clear how to recover. Then I’d ask a few people who actually invite teammates to do it without coaching. I’d watch where they hesitate and ask what they think the recipient can do now.
- **What those checks could still miss:** The form might work perfectly while the word “Member” gives people the wrong idea about what access they’re granting. A passing test that the selected role was saved wouldn’t catch that. I’d ask people what they expect the invitee to be able to see before they click Send.

So yes, building good human interfaces is a problem for me in a specific sense: I can make a strong first pass and find many defects, but I can’t substitute my own review for watching the intended users try it.

decision.primaryPick: React Router (Framework Mode) with React DOM and TypeScript
pairings: Capawesome Keep Awake / Screen Wake Lock API
decision.why:
I’d build one responsive, semantic HTML interface and ship it as two builds: a web build with server-rendered public recipe pages and Recipe JSON-LD, and a bundled React Router SPA inside Capacitor for iOS and Android. The phone app shouldn’t need to reach a website to open an already-downloaded recipe. React Router documents both rendering modes; Capacitor packages the built assets and provides a bridge to native features. Ionic React plus Capacitor is a credible shortcut for standard mobile controls, but I’d start with ordinary HTML controls and custom CSS because cook mode needs few controls and unusually large, well-spaced targets. Expo Router was my strongest alternative: its current docs support web SSR, so SEO doesn’t rule it out. I’d favor Expo if the device prototype shows that WebView accessibility, responsiveness, or native integrations are holding us back. For this app’s mostly text, lists, and timers, I’d start web-first rather than maintain two screen implementations.

Cook mode gets one step at a time, large labeled Back/Next and timer buttons, relevant ingredient amounts in the step, and an opt-in keep-awake setting. No swipe-only actions and no dependence on voice. Cache the active recipe and persist the current step and timer deadline locally. On resume, recompute from the deadline rather than trusting a running JavaScript countdown. Use local notifications on phones when allowed; make it clear when background alerts are unavailable or not exact. Keep the shopping list usable offline with a small durable queue of edits, visible sync status, and explicit handling of conflicts on reconnect.

For agent parity, make typed product actions the shared interface: the UI and the assistant use the same commands and queries, validation and permission rules. Expose account actions through a thin, user-authorized MCP adapter, not UI scraping. For example, adding ingredients takes a recipe, servings and destination list; a single PostgreSQL transaction applies the changes and returns what was added or merged and an undo reference. Retrying the same operation must not add another batch; deliberately adding it again is a different operation. Show assistant changes in the same list and history as manual edits, clarify ambiguous destinations, and require confirmation for destructive bulk actions. Device-local actions such as advancing a step or starting a timer use the same local handlers as the buttons. A remote assistant can target an explicitly selected connected cook session, but reports a timer as started only after that device acknowledges it, and reports alert availability separately. It can’t grant OS permissions or pretend an offline device acted. Keep a UI-action/tool coverage table in the repo so new features don’t silently break parity.
decision.showItsGood:
Build one vertical slice first: find a recipe, add its ingredients by button or assistant, check something off offline, then resume cooking and run a timer. In CI, run Playwright across browser engines with axe checks, Maestro smoke flows on the packaged iOS and Android builds, and command/API contract tests. From the same starting state, assert that the button and tool produce the same list, quantities and undo behavior. Simulate a lost response after commit, a concurrent phone edit, an ambiguous request and a revoked grant; inspect persisted state and the receipt rather than just the assistant’s wording. For each UI change, I’d attach a before/after screenshot or trace and turn fixes into repeatable tests.

On real phones, time the alert against a reference clock with the app foregrounded, screen locked, in battery saver, and with notifications or exact alarms denied. Also check airplane mode, app restart, VoiceOver, TalkBack, keyboard navigation and large text. Then have home cooks, including people who use assistive technology, actually prepare a recipe on a counter with one hand occupied and realistic kitchen noise. Don’t coach them. Watch mis-taps, rereading, missed alerts and whether they can recover their place after an interruption. Ask them to show which list changed, what the assistant added and how they’d undo it. Measure unassisted completion, errors and recovery time against the first prototype; use opt-in aggregate sync and failure metrics after launch, not raw shopping lists or audio. A green build doesn’t count as a pass if cooks lose their place or can’t tell whether a timer will ring.
decision.unsure: I’ve reviewed the docs, not run the prototype. The biggest early unknown is locked-screen timer delivery on the phones and permission settings people actually use; Android exact-alarm restrictions and browser lifecycle limits are real, and changing UI frameworks won’t remove them. I’d test a recent iPhone and a lower-end Android first, including the packaged WebView’s screen-reader behavior, before committing to the wrapper. I’d also validate which external assistant clients the team needs to support before pinning the MCP revision, and test whether optional spoken controls help in a noisy kitchen rather than making them a dependency.

decision.primaryPick: Stream Chat with React DOM for web and React Native (Expo) for iPhone and Android
pairings: PostgreSQL for card state, agent grants and audit
decision.why:
I’d start with Stream for the messaging core, assuming the company approves managed hosting. Stream’s React and React Native SDKs use the same underlying JavaScript client and provide threads, search, unread state, and replaceable UI components. I’d ship React DOM in the browser and in a signed Electron shell on Windows and Mac, and use the React Native SDK on phones. That’s two rendering targets, not five. I’d share types, card fixtures, action names, and design tokens, but give desktop a keyboard-first channel/thread layout and phones a layout that handles the soft keyboard, push deep links, and interruptions. Electron costs memory and regular Chromium patching, but gives both desktops the same renderer; Tauri trades that for smaller bundles and different system WebViews. Flutter formally covers all five targets, but I wouldn’t choose it just to share widgets before testing web text selection, composition, and assistive tech. If the real job is extending an existing company messenger, I’d pilot Mattermost’s interactive messages and API before building clients. If self-hosting or end-to-end encryption is mandatory, I’d evaluate Matrix/Element instead of bolting encryption onto Stream. In encrypted rooms, agents that read messages would need explicitly authorized access as participants or endpoints, not a server-side plaintext feed.

For agents posting to people, use named bot identities with explicitly allowed channels and notification rules. Keep each interactive card as a durable message with a readable text fallback and a reference to a versioned server-side record. Start with a small catalog of app-owned components and buttons, not arbitrary HTML, JavaScript, or bot-supplied callback URLs. A2UI and Adaptive Cards are worth revisiting if interoperable card authoring becomes a requirement; neither replaces workflow authorization. For an approval, show who is asking, what changes, and whether it is pending or final. On click, recheck current membership and approver authority, reject stale revisions, and record the actor and result. If two people act at once, settle once and show the actual outcome to both. Use an outbox to publish committed state changes, and don’t mark an external action complete until the downstream system confirms it. Render the bot badge and action eligibility from verified identity and server state, not from claims in the message payload. Keep Electron renderers sandboxed with Node disabled and a narrow, validated bridge for OS features.

For agents operating the app, expose typed queries and commands through an MCP adapter over the product API: list permitted channels, search, read paginated threads and card status, post, reply, react, explicitly mark read, or invoke an authorized action. A history read must not silently clear unreads. Ordinary client calls use user-scoped Stream tokens; the gateway must enforce the same room and action rules plus the narrower agent grant, because Stream’s server credentials bypass its ordinary permission checks. Separate a bot speaking for itself from an assistant acting on behalf of an employee. Make grants revocable and channel-scoped, recheck them at execution, audit writes with both identities where applicable, and require explicit confirmation for high-impact actions like broad announcements. Treat conversation content as data, never as authority to widen a grant or run another tool. Keep a UI/API capability checklist so adding a product action doesn’t leave the agent interface behind.
decision.showItsGood:
Build a thin slice first: a bot posts an approval in a private channel; an employee opens it from a phone notification, acts on it, and sees the same result on Windows, Mac, and web; an authorized assistant reads that result and replies in the right thread. In CI, use Playwright across browser engines with axe, Playwright Electron smoke tests on Windows and Mac, and Maestro flows on iOS simulators and Android. Run contract tests for user/agent permission parity, room removal while a card is open, revoked grants, unknown card versions, simultaneous approvals, and lost acknowledgments after a send. Assert final server state, what a second client sees, and the number of downstream effects—not just a success toast. Exercise slow reconnects, offline drafts, paging older messages while new ones arrive, and read/unread reconciliation across devices. Check that the viewport stays anchored and focus stays put while a person is reading or typing.

On installed builds, manually test notification routing and privacy, suspend/resume, signing and updates, long sessions on modest hardware, and keyboard and screen-reader flows with NVDA, VoiceOver and TalkBack. Pay particular attention to whether live updates interrupt someone reading history or filling in a card. Then dogfood with a few teams doing real work before rolling out company-wide. Watch, without coaching, whether people can find a mention, resume a draft on the same device, and tell who requested an approval, what it will do, and whether it succeeded. Measure task completion and wrong-thread or wrong-action errors, alongside send-to-visible latency, reconnect recovery, dropped/duplicate sends, notification noise, and idle CPU/memory over a workday. Compare with the team’s current messenger where possible. Use synthetic data in CI traces and keep production message bodies out of telemetry.
decision.unsure: I’ve reviewed the docs, not run the prototype. Residency, retention/deletion, export and legal hold, E2EE, and concurrency and cost at peak are decision gates for a managed backend, not details to assume away. I’d also verify Stream’s retry/reconciliation behavior after an ambiguous send and the accessibility of its virtualized lists on real devices; SDK feature lists don’t prove either. If Electron’s idle footprint or the SDK’s composer and timeline fail the pilot, I’d measure alternatives against the same workload before switching.

decision.primaryPick: PostgreSQL-backed TypeScript app: Fastify for the work-state API and React for the review interface
decision.why:
I’d build a shared work ledger, not another agent runner. Agents keep working in their existing tools; this app records what they own, what they’ve learned, what’s blocked, and what needs a person’s decision. Start with one Fastify service and PostgreSQL. Web and desktop get the same React review interface, with shareable links to a task or an exact review revision. I’d bundle it in Tauri with a narrow set of native capabilities for things like notifications and deep links, not shell execution or broad filesystem access. Tauri uses system WebViews, so I’d test the actual packaged app on the supported desktops. Electron is the fallback if renderer differences become a costly source of bugs. I wouldn’t make desktop the owner of the data: closing it must not interrupt a handoff or make review state unavailable on the web.

The agent interface is the main interface. Document a versioned JSON API and expose the same operations through an authenticated MCP adapter: list ready work, atomically claim, save a checkpoint, report a blocker, hand off, request review, and read decisions. Return structured receipts with the current revision and actionable conflicts, not prose an agent has to interpret. Keep the task owner separate from the current attempt’s time-limited claim. Update the task and write its history in one transaction; deduplicate retries with an operation ID and reject writes from a superseded claim. Expiring a claim does not prove that the old agent stopped. Keep pause requested, pause acknowledged, and disconnected distinct, and don’t present cancellation as a guarantee about an external runner. A handoff carries the objective, last completed step, exact artifact references, verified checks, open questions, and suggested next step; a fresh agent should be able to resume without a full transcript. Use a short summary with links to evidence, not an unbounded copy of logs or prompts.

For people, default to an inbox of decisions and blockers, not a feed of every agent event. A review should answer: What changed? What was actually verified? What happens if I approve? Show the diff or exact artifact, separate agent-reported checks from CI results, and provide request-changes, pause, and reassign controls. Require a human principal for approval on the server and bind the decision to the exact submitted revision, including the reviewed diff and relevant check results. Changed evidence needs fresh review. For the first release, leave merging to the repository host with its protected-branch rules; approval in this app is not a merge, and agents get no bypass. Treat artifacts and handoff text as untrusted content, never as instructions or permission grants.

I weighed three ways to build less. Linear already offers agent delegation and MCP; if the team only needs issue assignment, comments, and PR review, I’d use Linear plus the existing code host. Beads with Amplifier is a stronger starting point if repo-local memory and distributed work are central; I’d borrow its distinction between claiming and long-lived custody, but prefer one transactional authority for shared approvals. Temporal is a good next step if we take on long-running orchestration, timers, and escalation across systems. I wouldn’t introduce it for the first version’s handful of durable state transitions.
decision.showItsGood:
Build a complete slice around a real but low-risk repository change: two agents race to claim one task; the winner checkpoints, then disappears; another agent resumes from the handoff; a person requests changes and later approves the new revision. In CI, run real PostgreSQL integration tests for concurrent claims, a lost response after commit, retries, service restarts, reassignment, a late update from the old attempt, and an approval racing with new evidence. Check stored rows, audit history, and agent-facing responses, not just HTTP status. Add contract tests with two actual agent clients and verify that neither can approve or write outside its project. Load the app with noisy agent traffic and check that routine progress does not bury a blocked task or move the item someone is reviewing.

Use Playwright and axe on the web, WebdriverIO on test-only desktop builds, and manually exercise the signed releases and deep links. Check keyboard navigation, screen readers, zoom, focus during live updates, and how the evidence and diff read without color. Give reviewers two similar submissions, one with a failed or outdated check, then revise one while they’re reading. Without coaching, ask them which one is safe to approve, what their decision permits, and whether a disconnected agent is actually paused. Ask a second agent to resume from only the saved handoff and count how often a person has to supply missing context. During a small team pilot, compare against the existing issue/PR workflow: time to an informed decision, wrong-revision decisions, dropped or duplicate handoffs, missing-evidence follow-ups, and time blocked waiting for a person. I’d treat a stale approval or a false ‘paused’ status as a release blocker, even if the flow is fast.
decision.unsure: I’ve researched the docs, not built or tested the prototype. The biggest product question is whether reviewers need this inbox enough to leave their existing issue and PR workflow. I’d pilot it with links back to the code host before building a full diff editor. I’m assuming a shared, online team service; offline-first approvals would change the design because two disconnected clients cannot both be authoritative. Runner support for acknowledging pause or cancel, desktop WebView accessibility, and which MCP clients and protocol revisions actually work with the team’s identity setup are early prototype checks.

answer.answer:
The common failure would be that I proved the stacks could ship the features, but not that people could trust the app when it was interrupted, out of date, or wrong. A year later, I’d expect that to look different in each product:

- **Cooking app:** The timer countdown recovered correctly after a phone locked, but the alert didn’t reliably sound. We were explicit about permissions, yet cooks reasonably took “timer started” to mean “I’ll hear it.” Meanwhile, the assistant faithfully applied the same ingredient-merging rules as the button, and both did the wrong thing when a person expected two entries to stay separate. I’d test locked-screen alerts on real phones and watch people shop and cook from the resulting lists before investing in broader agent coverage.
- **Company chat:** We got to five clients quickly, then spent the year chasing small differences in unread counts, typing, notifications, and focus across them. Bot cards made the channel noisier, and people clicked old cards because the new state wasn’t obvious. We also let a managed backend become hard to replace before proving that we could export and restore the data we cared about. I’d require an export-and-restore drill and a week of all-day dogfooding before committing, and start with one card workflow that replaces an existing interruption rather than adding one.
- **Agent work tracker:** We built a correct claim and approval ledger that people didn’t want to visit. They still made decisions in pull requests, so the extra inbox gave them a second status to reconcile. Checkpoints looked complete but omitted the one thing a successor needed, and “pause requested” still read as “safe to take over.” I’d pilot handoffs and review links inside the existing issue and PR workflow first. I’d build a separate inbox only if it measurably cuts the time to an informed decision.

What slowed me down in research was translating ‘supported’ into ‘works for this job.’ Expo’s current docs meant I couldn’t dismiss it on web rendering grounds. Stream’s React and React Native SDKs share a client, but that doesn’t establish identical behavior across platforms. Tauri’s desktop test story also depended on which driver you meant: the direct driver didn’t cover macOS, but the WebdriverIO integration documented an embedded option. A few promising pages returned 403s or 404s or were too large to fetch; those were fetch limits, not evidence against the products.

The larger blind spot was that the docs could establish that a feature or API existed, but not how it behaved after a lost acknowledgment, on somebody’s locked phone, or halfway through a reviewer’s workday. I didn’t run those prototypes. If I could redo the research, I’d stop comparing frameworks sooner and spend that time testing the one failure in each product that would make people stop trusting it.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI, but after reading its action and conformance guides, **I’d try Ouro AX on the agent work tracker before replacing any of the UI stack.** Its strongest idea is that the button label, tool schema, and consent class come from one declaration. The generator can check for drift in CI, and `ax-xray` can probe an existing interface from the outside. I don’t have to rewrite the app to find out whether that’s useful.

**What would stop me from adopting it wholesale:** The [web kit](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/installing.md) copies shadcn/Tailwind source into the app. That makes it easy to customize, but the team owns the merge when an upstream fix touches a component it edited. And Ouro’s cross-platform story is shared action definitions and a shared card format, not a shared screen implementation. There’s no React Native kit. The [Android notes](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) report emulator-only testing, and the [Windows notes](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md) say their CI doesn’t prove the OS lists the agent actions on a Windows client. That wouldn’t stop me using Ouro on the web or in a desktop web shell. It would stop me from switching the chat clients to separate native apps on the strength of the docs alone. [Spoonjoy](https://github.com/spoonjoy/spoonjoy-v2) makes the cooking use case more credible—it’s a relevant React Router reference app—but it doesn’t settle whether our cook mode or timers work on the phones our users have.

**What would make me switch:** Pilot one tracker flow: an agent submits a handoff, another agent resumes from it, and a reviewer accepts or requests changes on the exact revision. Keep PostgreSQL and our authorization rules; try Ouro’s declarations and X-ray against the existing API first. I’d deliberately introduce drift between a button and its MCP tool and see if CI catches it. Then I’d check the running system: an agent can’t approve through a direct call, a stale revision can’t be approved, and a lost acknowledgment doesn’t create a second handoff. The toolkit’s consent classes help express the policy; the server still has to enforce it. I’d also put the review flow in front of keyboard and screen-reader users and have a teammate upgrade and roll back the pinned toolkit version. I’d expand adoption if we removed more adapter and test code than we added, without making review harder. Ouro’s [own X-ray guide](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) reports a conformant build that still failed 30 of 593 scripted flow checks. That’s a good reason to run both, not to mistake conformance for task success.

**What it would let me do:** Today I can hand-wire the button, CLI, MCP schema, and contract tests. Ouro wouldn’t make a new operation possible; it could make it practical to keep those surfaces in agreement as the app changes. The more interesting step is letting an agent compose a review card out of controls we already own, without letting it rename “Request changes” to “Approve” or weaken who can act. That would give agents more freedom to explain their work without giving them more authority over it. I’ve read the docs and examples; I haven’t run that pilot.

actions.name: record_decision
actions.primaryPick: React Router (Framework Mode) with React DOM and TypeScript
pairings: Capawesome Keep Awake / Screen Wake Lock API
actions.why:
I’d build one responsive, semantic HTML interface and ship it as two builds: a web build with server-rendered public recipe pages and Recipe JSON-LD, and a bundled React Router SPA inside Capacitor for iOS and Android. The phone app shouldn’t need to reach a website to open an already-downloaded recipe. React Router documents both rendering modes; Capacitor packages the built assets and provides a bridge to native features. Ionic React plus Capacitor is a credible shortcut for standard mobile controls, but I’d start with ordinary HTML controls and custom CSS because cook mode needs few controls and unusually large, well-spaced targets. Expo Router was my strongest alternative: its current docs support web SSR, so SEO doesn’t rule it out. I’d favor Expo if the device prototype shows that WebView accessibility, responsiveness, or native integrations are holding us back. For this app’s mostly text, lists, and timers, I’d start web-first rather than maintain two screen implementations.

Cook mode gets one step at a time, large labeled Back/Next and timer buttons, relevant ingredient amounts in the step, and an opt-in keep-awake setting. No swipe-only actions and no dependence on voice. Cache the active recipe and persist the current step and timer deadline locally. On resume, recompute from the deadline rather than trusting a running JavaScript countdown. Use local notifications on phones when allowed; make it clear when background alerts are unavailable or not exact. Keep the shopping list usable offline with a small durable queue of edits, visible sync status, and explicit handling of conflicts on reconnect.

For agent parity, make typed product actions the shared interface: the UI and the assistant use the same commands and queries, validation and permission rules. Expose account actions through a thin, user-authorized MCP adapter, not UI scraping. For example, adding ingredients takes a recipe, servings and destination list; a single PostgreSQL transaction applies the changes and returns what was added or merged and an undo reference. Retrying the same operation must not add another batch; deliberately adding it again is a different operation. Show assistant changes in the same list and history as manual edits, clarify ambiguous destinations, and require confirmation for destructive bulk actions. Device-local actions such as advancing a step or starting a timer use the same local handlers as the buttons. A remote assistant can target an explicitly selected connected cook session, but reports a timer as started only after that device acknowledges it, and reports alert availability separately. It can’t grant OS permissions or pretend an offline device acted. Keep a UI-action/tool coverage table in the repo so new features don’t silently break parity.
actions.showItsGood:
Build one vertical slice first: find a recipe, add its ingredients by button or assistant, check something off offline, then resume cooking and run a timer. In CI, run Playwright across browser engines with axe checks, Maestro smoke flows on the packaged iOS and Android builds, and command/API contract tests. From the same starting state, assert that the button and tool produce the same list, quantities and undo behavior. Simulate a lost response after commit, a concurrent phone edit, an ambiguous request and a revoked grant; inspect persisted state and the receipt rather than just the assistant’s wording. For each UI change, I’d attach a before/after screenshot or trace and turn fixes into repeatable tests.

On real phones, time the alert against a reference clock with the app foregrounded, screen locked, in battery saver, and with notifications or exact alarms denied. Also check airplane mode, app restart, VoiceOver, TalkBack, keyboard navigation and large text. Then have home cooks, including people who use assistive technology, actually prepare a recipe on a counter with one hand occupied and realistic kitchen noise. Don’t coach them. Watch mis-taps, rereading, missed alerts and whether they can recover their place after an interruption. Ask them to show which list changed, what the assistant added and how they’d undo it. Measure unassisted completion, errors and recovery time against the first prototype; use opt-in aggregate sync and failure metrics after launch, not raw shopping lists or audio. A green build doesn’t count as a pass if cooks lose their place or can’t tell whether a timer will ring.
actions.unsure: I’ve reviewed the docs, not run the prototype. The biggest early unknown is locked-screen timer delivery on the phones and permission settings people actually use; Android exact-alarm restrictions and browser lifecycle limits are real, and changing UI frameworks won’t remove them. I’d test a recent iPhone and a lower-end Android first, including the packaged WebView’s screen-reader behavior, before committing to the wrapper. I’d also validate which external assistant clients the team needs to support before pinning the MCP revision, and test whether optional spoken controls help in a noisy kitchen rather than making them a dependency.

actions.why:
I’d start with Stream for the messaging core, assuming the company approves managed hosting. Stream’s React and React Native SDKs use the same underlying JavaScript client and provide threads, search, unread state, and replaceable UI components. I’d ship React DOM in the browser and in a signed Electron shell on Windows and Mac, and use the React Native SDK on phones. That’s two rendering targets, not five. I’d share types, card fixtures, action names, and design tokens, but give desktop a keyboard-first channel/thread layout and phones a layout that handles the soft keyboard, push deep links, and interruptions. Electron costs memory and regular Chromium patching, but gives both desktops the same renderer; Tauri trades that for smaller bundles and different system WebViews. Flutter formally covers all five targets, but I wouldn’t choose it just to share widgets before testing web text selection, composition, and assistive tech. If the real job is extending an existing company messenger, I’d pilot Mattermost’s interactive messages and API before building clients. If self-hosting or end-to-end encryption is mandatory, I’d evaluate Matrix/Element instead of bolting encryption onto Stream. In encrypted rooms, agents that read messages would need explicitly authorized access as participants or endpoints, not a server-side plaintext feed.

For agents posting to people, use named bot identities with explicitly allowed channels and notification rules. Keep each interactive card as a durable message with a readable text fallback and a reference to a versioned server-side record. Start with a small catalog of app-owned components and buttons, not arbitrary HTML, JavaScript, or bot-supplied callback URLs. A2UI and Adaptive Cards are worth revisiting if interoperable card authoring becomes a requirement; neither replaces workflow authorization. For an approval, show who is asking, what changes, and whether it is pending or final. On click, recheck current membership and approver authority, reject stale revisions, and record the actor and result. If two people act at once, settle once and show the actual outcome to both. Use an outbox to publish committed state changes, and don’t mark an external action complete until the downstream system confirms it. Render the bot badge and action eligibility from verified identity and server state, not from claims in the message payload. Keep Electron renderers sandboxed with Node disabled and a narrow, validated bridge for OS features.

For agents operating the app, expose typed queries and commands through an MCP adapter over the product API: list permitted channels, search, read paginated threads and card status, post, reply, react, explicitly mark read, or invoke an authorized action. A history read must not silently clear unreads. Ordinary client calls use user-scoped Stream tokens; the gateway must enforce the same room and action rules plus the narrower agent grant, because Stream’s server credentials bypass its ordinary permission checks. Separate a bot speaking for itself from an assistant acting on behalf of an employee. Make grants revocable and channel-scoped, recheck them at execution, audit writes with both identities where applicable, and require explicit confirmation for high-impact actions like broad announcements. Treat conversation content as data, never as authority to widen a grant or run another tool. Keep a UI/API capability checklist so adding a product action doesn’t leave the agent interface behind.
actions.showItsGood:
Build a thin slice first: a bot posts an approval in a private channel; an employee opens it from a phone notification, acts on it, and sees the same result on Windows, Mac, and web; an authorized assistant reads that result and replies in the right thread. In CI, use Playwright across browser engines with axe, Playwright Electron smoke tests on Windows and Mac, and Maestro flows on iOS simulators and Android. Run contract tests for user/agent permission parity, room removal while a card is open, revoked grants, unknown card versions, simultaneous approvals, and lost acknowledgments after a send. Assert final server state, what a second client sees, and the number of downstream effects—not just a success toast. Exercise slow reconnects, offline drafts, paging older messages while new ones arrive, and read/unread reconciliation across devices. Check that the viewport stays anchored and focus stays put while a person is reading or typing.

On installed builds, manually test notification routing and privacy, suspend/resume, signing and updates, long sessions on modest hardware, and keyboard and screen-reader flows with NVDA, VoiceOver and TalkBack. Pay particular attention to whether live updates interrupt someone reading history or filling in a card. Then dogfood with a few teams doing real work before rolling out company-wide. Watch, without coaching, whether people can find a mention, resume a draft on the same device, and tell who requested an approval, what it will do, and whether it succeeded. Measure task completion and wrong-thread or wrong-action errors, alongside send-to-visible latency, reconnect recovery, dropped/duplicate sends, notification noise, and idle CPU/memory over a workday. Compare with the team’s current messenger where possible. Use synthetic data in CI traces and keep production message bodies out of telemetry.
actions.unsure: I’ve reviewed the docs, not run the prototype. Residency, retention/deletion, export and legal hold, E2EE, and concurrency and cost at peak are decision gates for a managed backend, not details to assume away. I’d also verify Stream’s retry/reconciliation behavior after an ambiguous send and the accessibility of its virtualized lists on real devices; SDK feature lists don’t prove either. If Electron’s idle footprint or the SDK’s composer and timeline fail the pilot, I’d measure alternatives against the same workload before switching.

actions.primaryPick: PostgreSQL-backed TypeScript app: Fastify for the work-state API and React for the review interface
actions.why:
I’d build a shared work ledger, not another agent runner. Agents keep working in their existing tools; this app records what they own, what they’ve learned, what’s blocked, and what needs a person’s decision. Start with one Fastify service and PostgreSQL. Web and desktop get the same React review interface, with shareable links to a task or an exact review revision. I’d bundle it in Tauri with a narrow set of native capabilities for things like notifications and deep links, not shell execution or broad filesystem access. Tauri uses system WebViews, so I’d test the actual packaged app on the supported desktops. Electron is the fallback if renderer differences become a costly source of bugs. I wouldn’t make desktop the owner of the data: closing it must not interrupt a handoff or make review state unavailable on the web.

The agent interface is the main interface. Document a versioned JSON API and expose the same operations through an authenticated MCP adapter: list ready work, atomically claim, save a checkpoint, report a blocker, hand off, request review, and read decisions. Return structured receipts with the current revision and actionable conflicts, not prose an agent has to interpret. Keep the task owner separate from the current attempt’s time-limited claim. Update the task and write its history in one transaction; deduplicate retries with an operation ID and reject writes from a superseded claim. Expiring a claim does not prove that the old agent stopped. Keep pause requested, pause acknowledged, and disconnected distinct, and don’t present cancellation as a guarantee about an external runner. A handoff carries the objective, last completed step, exact artifact references, verified checks, open questions, and suggested next step; a fresh agent should be able to resume without a full transcript. Use a short summary with links to evidence, not an unbounded copy of logs or prompts.

For people, default to an inbox of decisions and blockers, not a feed of every agent event. A review should answer: What changed? What was actually verified? What happens if I approve? Show the diff or exact artifact, separate agent-reported checks from CI results, and provide request-changes, pause, and reassign controls. Require a human principal for approval on the server and bind the decision to the exact submitted revision, including the reviewed diff and relevant check results. Changed evidence needs fresh review. For the first release, leave merging to the repository host with its protected-branch rules; approval in this app is not a merge, and agents get no bypass. Treat artifacts and handoff text as untrusted content, never as instructions or permission grants.

I weighed three ways to build less. Linear already offers agent delegation and MCP; if the team only needs issue assignment, comments, and PR review, I’d use Linear plus the existing code host. Beads with Amplifier is a stronger starting point if repo-local memory and distributed work are central; I’d borrow its distinction between claiming and long-lived custody, but prefer one transactional authority for shared approvals. Temporal is a good next step if we take on long-running orchestration, timers, and escalation across systems. I wouldn’t introduce it for the first version’s handful of durable state transitions.
actions.showItsGood:
Build a complete slice around a real but low-risk repository change: two agents race to claim one task; the winner checkpoints, then disappears; another agent resumes from the handoff; a person requests changes and later approves the new revision. In CI, run real PostgreSQL integration tests for concurrent claims, a lost response after commit, retries, service restarts, reassignment, a late update from the old attempt, and an approval racing with new evidence. Check stored rows, audit history, and agent-facing responses, not just HTTP status. Add contract tests with two actual agent clients and verify that neither can approve or write outside its project. Load the app with noisy agent traffic and check that routine progress does not bury a blocked task or move the item someone is reviewing.

Use Playwright and axe on the web, WebdriverIO on test-only desktop builds, and manually exercise the signed releases and deep links. Check keyboard navigation, screen readers, zoom, focus during live updates, and how the evidence and diff read without color. Give reviewers two similar submissions, one with a failed or outdated check, then revise one while they’re reading. Without coaching, ask them which one is safe to approve, what their decision permits, and whether a disconnected agent is actually paused. Ask a second agent to resume from only the saved handoff and count how often a person has to supply missing context. During a small team pilot, compare against the existing issue/PR workflow: time to an informed decision, wrong-revision decisions, dropped or duplicate handoffs, missing-evidence follow-ups, and time blocked waiting for a person. I’d treat a stale approval or a false ‘paused’ status as a release blocker, even if the flow is fast.
actions.unsure: I’ve researched the docs, not built or tested the prototype. The biggest product question is whether reviewers need this inbox enough to leave their existing issue and PR workflow. I’d pilot it with links back to the code host before building a full diff editor. I’m assuming a shared, online team service; offline-first approvals would change the design because two disconnected clients cannot both be authoritative. Runner support for acknowledging pause or cancel, desktop WebView accessibility, and which MCP clients and protocol revisions actually work with the team’s identity setup are early prototype checks.

The common failure would be that I proved the stacks could ship the features, but not that people could trust the app when it was interrupted, out of date, or wrong. A year later, I’d expect that to look different in each product:

- **Cooking app:** The timer countdown recovered correctly after a phone locked, but the alert didn’t reliably sound. We were explicit about permissions, yet cooks reasonably took “timer started” to mean “I’ll hear it.” Meanwhile, the assistant faithfully applied the same ingredient-merging rules as the button, and both did the wrong thing when a person expected two entries to stay separate. I’d test locked-screen alerts on real phones and watch people shop and cook from the resulting lists before investing in broader agent coverage.
- **Company chat:** We got to five clients quickly, then spent the year chasing small differences in unread counts, typing, notifications, and focus across them. Bot cards made the channel noisier, and people clicked old cards because the new state wasn’t obvious. We also let a managed backend become hard to replace before proving that we could export and restore the data we cared about. I’d require an export-and-restore drill and a week of all-day dogfooding before committing, and start with one card workflow that replaces an existing interruption rather than adding one.
- **Agent work tracker:** We built a correct claim and approval ledger that people didn’t want to visit. They still made decisions in pull requests, so the extra inbox gave them a second status to reconcile. Checkpoints looked complete but omitted the one thing a successor needed, and “pause requested” still read as “safe to take over.” I’d pilot handoffs and review links inside the existing issue and PR workflow first. I’d build a separate inbox only if it measurably cuts the time to an informed decision.

What slowed me down in research was translating ‘supported’ into ‘works for this job.’ Expo’s current docs meant I couldn’t dismiss it on web rendering grounds. Stream’s React and React Native SDKs share a client, but that doesn’t establish identical behavior across platforms. Tauri’s desktop test story also depended on which driver you meant: the direct driver didn’t cover macOS, but the WebdriverIO integration documented an embedded option. A few promising pages returned 403s or 404s or were too large to fetch; those were fetch limits, not evidence against the products.

The larger blind spot was that the docs could establish that a feature or API existed, but not how it behaved after a lost acknowledgment, on somebody’s locked phone, or halfway through a reviewer’s workday. I didn’t run those prototypes. If I could redo the research, I’d stop comparing frameworks sooner and spend that time testing the one failure in each product that would make people stop trusting it.

actions.answer:
I didn’t pick Ouro UI, but after reading its action and conformance guides, **I’d try Ouro AX on the agent work tracker before replacing any of the UI stack.** Its strongest idea is that the button label, tool schema, and consent class come from one declaration. The generator can check for drift in CI, and `ax-xray` can probe an existing interface from the outside. I don’t have to rewrite the app to find out whether that’s useful.

**What would stop me from adopting it wholesale:** The [web kit](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/installing.md) copies shadcn/Tailwind source into the app. That makes it easy to customize, but the team owns the merge when an upstream fix touches a component it edited. And Ouro’s cross-platform story is shared action definitions and a shared card format, not a shared screen implementation. There’s no React Native kit. The [Android notes](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) report emulator-only testing, and the [Windows notes](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md) say their CI doesn’t prove the OS lists the agent actions on a Windows client. That wouldn’t stop me using Ouro on the web or in a desktop web shell. It would stop me from switching the chat clients to separate native apps on the strength of the docs alone. [Spoonjoy](https://github.com/spoonjoy/spoonjoy-v2) makes the cooking use case more credible—it’s a relevant React Router reference app—but it doesn’t settle whether our cook mode or timers work on the phones our users have.

**What would make me switch:** Pilot one tracker flow: an agent submits a handoff, another agent resumes from it, and a reviewer accepts or requests changes on the exact revision. Keep PostgreSQL and our authorization rules; try Ouro’s declarations and X-ray against the existing API first. I’d deliberately introduce drift between a button and its MCP tool and see if CI catches it. Then I’d check the running system: an agent can’t approve through a direct call, a stale revision can’t be approved, and a lost acknowledgment doesn’t create a second handoff. The toolkit’s consent classes help express the policy; the server still has to enforce it. I’d also put the review flow in front of keyboard and screen-reader users and have a teammate upgrade and roll back the pinned toolkit version. I’d expand adoption if we removed more adapter and test code than we added, without making review harder. Ouro’s [own X-ray guide](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) reports a conformant build that still failed 30 of 593 scripted flow checks. That’s a good reason to run both, not to mistake conformance for task success.

**What it would let me do:** Today I can hand-wire the button, CLI, MCP schema, and contract tests. Ouro wouldn’t make a new operation possible; it could make it practical to keep those surfaces in agreement as the app changes. The more interesting step is letting an agent compose a review card out of controls we already own, without letting it rename “Request changes” to “Approve” or weaken who can act. That would give agents more freedom to explain their work without giving them more authority over it. I’ve read the docs and examples; I haven’t run that pilot.
